lessons.title: From Broken Kid to Navy SEAL
lessons.key_idea: Your past may explain where you are, but you still have the power to rewrite where you're going.

lessons.title: Face the Accountability Mirror
lessons.key_idea: Real change starts when you tell yourself the raw truth about your life and write down exactly what must change.

lessons.title: Callus Your Mind
lessons.key_idea: Doing hard, uncomfortable things on purpose toughens your mind the way repeated friction toughens skin.
issues: scene 7: The 'WAIT FOR LIFE' sign has a strike line through the middle of its letters, so the label is hard to read. The signpost pole also cuts through the right end of the grey sign box. (fix: Keep the label readable: grey it out or put a small X beside it instead of striking through the text. Move the grey sign so its right edge ends at the pole, mirroring the amber sign.)

scene 8: The checklist illustration sits almost on top of the 'visualgrowth.app' footer at the bottom right, with only a few pixels between them. (fix: Move the checklist up by about 40px, or shrink it slightly, so there is clear space between it and the footer.)

lessons.title: Reach Into the Cookie Jar
lessons.key_idea: When you're struggling, remembering the hard things you've already overcome gives you fuel to keep going.
issues: scene 1: The cookie icon and arrow in the bottom-right corner sit directly above the 'visualgrowth.app' brand label and nearly touch it. The corner looks crowded and the elements read as stacked. (fix: Move the arrow and cookie up and left, for example aligned with the 'What matters is what you reach for next.' line ending around x≈1250, leaving at least 40px clearance above the brand label.)

scene 1: The running stick figure's pose reads as broken. The rear leg kinks sharply backward from the knee, and the arms are short disconnected stubs, so it looks malformed rather than like someone straining mid-run. (fix: Redraw the figure with a clear running pose: both legs bent at the knee with one forward, arms bent and attached at the shoulder, and a slight forward lean to suggest struggle.)

lessons.title: The 40 Percent Rule
lessons.key_idea: When your mind says you're done, you've usually used only about 40 percent of what you're capable of.
issues: scene 1: The strikethrough crosses out only 'I'm finished.' and leaves 'I have nothing left.' untouched, so the bubble suggests the first claim is false and the second is true. The strike line also runs past the end of the text. (fix: Show both lines plainly while the voice is speaking, then strike both together (or neither) when 'lying' appears. Trim the strike line to the text width.)

scene 3: The third panel's 'brakes' drawing is a bare pole with a tilted bar. It reads as a hammer or a lever, not a brake. The brakes-versus-danger track below it is too small to carry the idea. (fix: Replace it with a recognisable brake pedal or a stop sign. Make the track larger: put a 'brakes' marker early on the line and a 'real danger' marker far right, with a shaded gap between them to show braking happens long before danger.)

scene 4: The 'big lifter' figure looks like a person sitting behind a table. The barbell is not recognisable. (fix: Draw a figure holding a barbell overhead or across the shoulders, with clear weight plates at both ends of the bar.)

lessons.title: Fail Forward With an After-Action Report
lessons.key_idea: Failure becomes useful when you study it honestly, fix what went wrong, and try again.

lessons.title: Become Uncommon Among the Uncommon
lessons.key_idea: Lasting growth comes from never settling, staying hungry, and using every tool daily to keep pushing your limits.

plan.title: Can't Hurt Me
plan.author: David Goggins
plan.confidence_note: I know this memoir and its core challenges well, including the Accountability Mirror, the Cookie Jar and the 40 Percent Rule, though I would avoid quoting exact figures I can't verify.
plan.one_liner: How an abused, overweight kid rebuilt his mind and became one of the world's toughest men.
plan.summary: David Goggins grew up with an abusive father, poverty, racism and learning struggles. In his twenties he was nearly 300 pounds, working a dead-end job spraying for pests and feeling like a failure. Then he decided to change. He lost over 100 pounds to qualify for Navy SEAL training, survived multiple Hell Weeks, and went on to run brutal ultramarathons and set a pull-up record. Part memoir, part challenge, the book argues that most of us live far below our potential because our minds quit long before our bodies must. Goggins shares the mental tools he built along the way: facing hard truths, seeking discomfort on purpose, drawing strength from past wins, and treating failure as data. Each chapter ends with a challenge for the reader.
